title: Slow-Roast Pork Belly with Crackling
subtitle: Long-roasted pork belly, basted and crisped
excerpt: Pork belly slow-roasted for three hours until the fat is rendered and the meat is soft, then blasted at high heat for crackling that shatters. The two-stage method gives you perfect crackling without dry meat.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pork belly has been roasted in Britain for centuries, originally a practical choice for a cut that is cheap, fatty, and forgiving. The crackling technique, scoring the rind deeply and salting it overnight, was documented in Victorian cookery writing. The two-stage cooking method is the modern approach: slow roasting renders the fat and tenderises the meat without drying it, then a high blast at the end converts the rind to crackling. It is associated with Sunday roast culture and pub dining.

content.text: Score the rind deeply with a sharp knife or Stanley knife: cut right down through the rind but not into the meat below. The cuts should be 1 cm apart. Leave uncovered in the fridge overnight: the dry fridge air removes surface moisture from the rind, which is what allows it to crisp rather than steam. Season generously with salt and nothing else on the rind.

The day before: pat the pork belly dry. Score the rind at 1 cm intervals. Rub the rind with oil and a generous amount of sea salt flakes, making sure the salt gets into all the cuts. Leave uncovered in the fridge overnight.

Remove the pork from the fridge 1 hour before cooking. Heat the oven to 160 C / fan 140 C / gas 3. Put the garlic, thyme, and fennel seeds in the roasting tin and rest the pork rind-side up on top. Add 100 ml water to the tin. Roast for 2.5 to 3 hours until the meat is very tender when pierced.

Increase the oven to 240 C / fan 220 C / gas 9. Roast for 20 to 30 minutes more, watching closely, until the crackling is puffed and blistered and completely crisp. If any patches remain soft, use a kitchen blowtorch or move under the grill.
Rest for 15 minutes before cutting. Slice between the score marks to separate crackling strips with the meat underneath.
